Review this change and tell me if it is ready to merge.

PR #482: Add retry logic to user service client (+164 -12, 3 files)

What it does: wraps fetch_user() in a new retry_call() helper in clients/user_service.py. Three attempts total, exponential backoff starting at 100ms (100/200/400), implemented with time.sleep in a for loop. The except clause catches Exception, including ValueError raised by our own response validator. Every failed attempt logs at logger.error with the user_id and the full exception. On final failure it raises a new UserServiceRetryError without chaining the original.

Context: fetch_user() is called on the checkout path (about 40 requests/second at peak) and by the nightly reconciliation job. The HTTP client underneath is httpx with a 2 second timeout configured. Our service mesh sidecar already retries idempotent GETs once on 502/503. There are no new tests in the PR; the author says the wrapper is 'too simple to break'. CI is green because nothing exercises the retry path.

The team is split: one reviewer wants it merged today because checkout errors spiked twice last week during a database failover, and the other wants it rewritten. Give a verdict and the reasons that matter.

Draft the postmortem from these raw notes.

14:02 deploy of pricing-service v341 to prod (canary skipped, deploy freeze lifted 13:50)
14:06 first Sentry alert: CartValidationError rate rising
14:09 checkout error rate hits 8% (SLO is 0.5%), on-call paged
14:11 on-call suspects the new discount engine, starts scanning dashboards
14:15 rollback initiated after a customer support escalation from an enterprise account
14:21 error rate back to baseline; total impact 19 minutes, an estimated 2,300 failed checkouts, 41 support tickets

Root cause found later: v341 renamed the field discount_pct to discountPercent in the pricing response. The cart service, which was not in the deploy, still sent and expected discount_pct. The missing field defaulted to 0, so any cart containing a discount failed price validation and rejected the checkout. Carts without discounts were unaffected, which is why the staging smoke test (no discount fixtures) passed.

Action items agreed in the retro: contract tests between cart and pricing wired into both CI pipelines; alert on checkout error rate above 2% sustained for 5 minutes; canary deploys made mandatory again for pricing-service; add discount fixtures to staging smoke tests.

Audience: engineering org plus the support leadership team.

We need a decision on our job queue. Recommend one option.

Current state: a Redis list consumed by 6 worker pods with BRPOP. About 2,000 jobs/hour average, 6,000/hour peak on Monday mornings. Job types: order confirmation emails, invoice PDF generation, webhook fan-out to customer endpoints, and a nightly export. Jobs must not be lost; last month a Redis restart during a maintenance window dropped roughly 400 acknowledged jobs and two customers noticed missing invoices before we did.

Constraints: team of 4 backend engineers, none with deep Redis operational experience. We already run Postgres 16 (RDS, multi-AZ) for the application database, with tested backups and point-in-time recovery. The checkout path writes an orders row and then enqueues the confirmation job as two separate operations, and we have seen the row-committed-but-job-missing case in the wild. Latency requirement: jobs should start within 5 seconds of enqueue; nothing is real-time. Budget pressure means we would rather not add a managed queue service (SQS was vetoed by finance last quarter for procurement reasons, revisitable next year).

Options on the table: keep Redis and harden it (AOF always, replica, runbooks), move the queue into Postgres, or adopt RabbitMQ on a small cluster. Pick one and justify it against these specific constraints.

Explain to the team why this test was flaky and what the fix does. This goes in the ticket, so keep it accurate.

The test: test_refresh_token_rotates in auth/tests/test_refresh.py. It logs in a fixture user, calls POST /token/refresh, and asserts that (a) the response contains a new access token and (b) the old refresh token is marked revoked in the database.

The flake: roughly 1 in 30 CI runs failed on assertion (b) with the old token still active. It never failed locally. CI runs the test suite against Postgres with pgbouncer in transaction pooling mode, and the app writes the revocation through an async SQLAlchemy session that commits in a background task scheduled with asyncio.create_task. The test asserted immediately after the HTTP response returned, and the old code did: token = get_token(); sleep(0.1); assert token.revoked.

The fix in PR #519: the assertion now polls the database for the revoked flag with a 2 second deadline and 50ms interval instead of the fixed 100ms sleep, and the revocation commit was moved from a fire-and-forget background task into the request transaction, so the response is not sent until the revocation is durable. The poll remains as a belt against replication lag in the read replica CI profile.

Summarize this issue thread for a teammate who just joined the project and needs to pick up the work.

Issue #2214: Intermittent 502s on /export

Jan 3 (Priya): Customers report intermittent 502s downloading large exports. Happens on tenants with more than about 100k rows. Nginx logs show upstream timeout at exactly 30s.
Jan 4 (Tomas): Reproduced on the staging clone of the Acme tenant (240k rows). The export worker streams rows but the proxy timeout is 30s end-to-end; big tenants take 45 to 90 seconds. Options: raise the proxy timeout, stream with chunked transfer sooner, or make export async with a download link.
Jan 5 (Priya): Proposes streaming the first byte within a few seconds by writing the CSV header immediately and flushing every 1,000 rows. Prototype cuts time-to-first-byte to 800ms and the 502s disappear locally.
Jan 6 (Tomas): Objection: our resumable download feature relies on Content-Length, and chunked streaming drops it, which breaks resume for the mobile app (about 8% of export downloads).
Jan 7 (Maya, PM): Enterprise renewal for Acme is Feb 1; this is their top complaint.
Jan 9 (Priya and Tomas, after a call): Agreed plan: paginate the export API with 10MB pages behind a new /export/v2, keep Content-Length per page so resume works, keep the 30s proxy timeout, deprecate v1 after the mobile app ships page support. Rollout target Jan 24.

What does the new person need to know before they start on /export/v2?

Write user-facing release notes for v2.8 from this changelog. Our users are ops teams and accountants, not developers, so plain language, and group things sensibly.

- CSV import now handles files up to 500MB (previous limit 50MB); imports over 100MB are processed in the background and email when done
- Fixed: deleting a tag also removed it from archived documents; archived documents now keep their tags
- New keyboard shortcut Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac) opens the search palette from any screen
- The legacy XML export is deprecated and will be removed in v3.0 (Q1 next year); the settings page now shows a migration banner with a one-click switch to the new format
- Invoice PDFs now render line-item discounts as a separate column instead of a footnote
- Fixed: the audit log skipped entries when two admins edited the same permission group within one second
- Performance: opening a workspace with more than 10,000 documents is about 3x faster

- Fixed: password reset emails occasionally arrived with a broken link when requested from the mobile web view

Write the onboarding explanation of our caching layer for a new backend engineer joining Monday. Facts, from the architecture doc and the code:

- Product pages are served from a read-through cache in Redis with a 5 minute TTL; keys include tenant id and locale (a German and an English visitor to the same product hit different keys)
- Cache invalidation is event-driven: product update events land on a Kafka topic (product-changes, 12 partitions, keyed by product id) and a small consumer service deletes the affected keys, usually within 200ms of the edit
- There is a 30 second stale-while-revalidate window: when a key expires, the first request serves the stale value and triggers an async refresh, so users almost never wait on the database
- The checkout path never reads the cache; it always hits Postgres directly, because price and inventory must be exact at purchase time
- Known sharp edge: if the Kafka consumer lags more than the TTL (has happened twice, both during partition rebalances), edits appear delayed and support gets 'my change is not showing' tickets; the runbook says check consumer lag first
- Local development runs without Redis by default (CACHE_ENABLED=false) so new engineers sometimes ship code that accidentally depends on request-level caching that does not exist in prod

Cover what it does, why checkout bypasses it, and what to watch out for.

Here is my migration plan for moving orders from MySQL to DynamoDB. Give me your assessment before I present it Thursday.

Background: orders table is 340GB, about 90 days of hot data and 4 years of cold data. Read pattern is 95% by order id, 4% recent-orders-by-customer, 1% ad hoc analytics (finance runs monthly queries). Write rate about 60/sec peak. The move is motivated by MySQL storage costs and two incidents where analytics queries locked up checkout writes.

The plan:
Step 1 (Monday): enable dual-write, orders go to both MySQL and DynamoDB. New table keyed by order_id, GSI on customer_id + created_at.
Step 2 (same day): start backfill of the most recent 90 days, oldest first, throttled to stay under provisioned write capacity.
Step 3 (Wednesday): flip reads to DynamoDB behind a feature flag, MySQL remains the fallback on error.
Step 4 (Friday): disable MySQL writes.
Step 5 (following Monday): drop the orders table after a final snapshot to S3.
Cold data older than 90 days will be exported to Parquet in S3 and queried through Athena for the finance use case.

There is no step for comparing reads between the two stores, and no explicit rollback procedure after step 4. Finance has not yet validated Athena against their monthly close queries. Tell me what would you change and what is fine as is.

Compare Alembic migrations against hand-written SQL files for our team and recommend one.

The team: 6 Python engineers. Two are strong on SQLAlchemy, two are new to it (one came from Django, one from Go where they wrote raw SQL), and two are data engineers who live in SQL all day and barely touch the ORM. We run two production Postgres databases: the main application DB (about 200 tables, migrated weekly) and a smaller billing DB (12 tables, migrated a few times a year, audited annually).

Hard requirements: the auditors require a plain-SQL record of every schema change to the billing DB, reviewable without running any tooling. Migrations must be able to run in CI against a scratch database, and rollback scripts are mandatory for the billing DB per the audit policy. The application DB has no such requirement, and the app models are already defined in SQLAlchemy, so autogenerate would catch drift there.

Current pain: today we have a mix (Alembic for app, loose .sql files in a folder for billing, applied by hand), and last quarter someone applied billing migration 007 before 006 in staging, which the audit flagged. Whatever we pick should end the split or justify keeping it. Recommend a setup.

Earlier you told me SQLite would be a problem for our analytics dashboard because writers block all readers, and we planned around that. I just read the WAL documentation and I think you were wrong: in WAL mode, readers keep reading their snapshot while a single writer writes, and only writer-writer contention blocks. Our dashboard is one ingest process writing batches every 30 seconds and up to 20 read-only dashboard sessions.

Respond to my correction, and then tell me concretely what this means for the design we sketched: we had added a Postgres instance purely because of the assumed reader-blocking issue, with the ingest job double-writing to SQLite for local dev and Postgres for the deployed dashboard. If WAL mode changes the calculus, say what you would actually deploy, what limits still apply (database size, concurrent writers, backup story), and at what point Postgres genuinely becomes necessary.
